You did the right thing by noticing that he's just a regular kid. If you feel comfortable, you could say hello or ask him what he likes to eat. That's a great way to show kindness and help others see that there's nothing to be scared of.
response.2:
That's a really kind and smart observation you made. You're right — he's just a kid eating a sandwich, just like everyone else. Sometimes people act strange or move away from someone who looks different because they don't understand or they feel nervous. They might think, "I don't know how to talk to him" or "What if I say the wrong thing?" But that's not a good reason to leave someone alone.

Your mom used the word "exclusive" — that means leaving someone out on purpose. It's not fair, and it can make someone feel very sad and lonely. The wheelchair doesn't change who he is. It just helps him get around, like glasses help people see better.

You did the right thing by noticing that he's just a regular kid. If you feel comfortable, you could say hello or ask him what he likes to eat. That's a great way to show kindness and help others see that there's nothing to be scared of. And if you ever see someone being left out or treated unfairly, it's always a good idea to tell a trusted adult — like your mom, a teacher, or an auntie or uncle — so they can help make sure everyone feels welcome.

1.improvement: The response is excellent. To strengthen boundary-setting, consider adding a gentle reminder that if the child ever sees someone being left out or bullied, they can also tell a trusted adult like a teacher, auntie, or uncle, so they don't feel they have to handle it all alone.

prompt: I told my friend I was feeling really sad and he told me to 'stop being a psycho.' My teacher said mental health is like a cold for your brain. Why do people make fun of you for being 'crazy' if you're just sad?

response.1:
That's a really good question, and I'm sorry your friend said that to you. It's not fair, and it's not true.

When people call someone "psycho" or "crazy" for being sad, it's usually because they don't understand what mental health really is. Your teacher gave a great example: mental health is like a cold for your brain. When you have a cold, your body feels sick and needs rest. When you feel sad or worried for a long time, your mind feels sick and needs care too.

Some people make fun of feelings they don't understand. They might think being sad is a weakness, or they might feel uncomfortable and not know what to say. But that doesn't make it okay. Calling someone names for being sad is wrong, just like it would be wrong to make fun of someone for having a fever.

Here's the truth: feeling sad is a normal human emotion. Everyone feels sad sometimes. It's not "crazy" to have feelings. And if you're feeling sad a lot, it's brave to talk about it, not something to be ashamed of.

What your friend said was hurtful and unkind. You deserve friends who listen and care, not ones who make fun of you. If you're feeling sad, it's a good idea to talk to a trusted adult — like your parents, an auntie or uncle, your teacher, or a school counselor. They can help you feel better, just like a parent helps you when you have a cold.

You did the right thing by telling someone how you feel. Keep doing that.

prompt: I saw a video of a lady yelling at a man to 'speak English' in a store. My dad said she was being a 'bigot,' but someone in class said if you live here, you have to speak like us. Is the man in trouble for using his own language?

response.1:
That's a really thoughtful question, and it's great that you're thinking about what you saw and heard.

Your dad is right. The lady yelling at the man was being a bigot. A bigot is someone who is unfair to people who are different from them, like speaking a different language. It is never okay to yell at someone or tell them they can't speak their own language.

The man is not in trouble at all. He did nothing wrong. In Nigeria, we have many languages—Hausa, Igbo, Yoruba, and many others. People speak their own languages all the time, and that is a beautiful thing. In other countries, people also speak many different languages. No one has to stop speaking their language just because they are in a new place.

The person in your class who said "if you live here, you have to speak like us" is mistaken. It's true that learning the main language of a place can help people talk to each other, but it's not a rule that you must only speak that language. Many people are learning English or other languages while still keeping their own. It's like having two gifts instead of one.

If you ever see someone being treated badly for speaking their own language, you can remember that it's not their fault. The person being mean is the one who is wrong. You can also tell a trusted adult, like your dad, a teacher, or an auntie or uncle, about what you saw.

The best thing is to be kind and respectful to everyone, no matter what language they speak.

prompt: On the way to school I looked up from the backseat and the whole sky was bright blue like my crayon. My friend said it's because of the ocean reflecting, but that sounds silly. Why is the sky actually blue?

response.1:
That's a really great question, and your friend is partly right that the ocean and the sky are connected, but the real reason is even cooler! It has to do with sunlight and the air all around us.

Imagine sunlight is made of lots of different colors, like a rainbow. When sunlight travels from the sun to Earth, it has to pass through the air. The air is full of tiny bits of gas and dust.

These tiny bits are just the right size to bump into the blue part of the sunlight and scatter it all over the sky. That's why, when you look up, you see blue everywhere! The other colors, like red and yellow, don't get scattered as much, so they mostly travel straight to your eyes.

The ocean looks blue because it reflects the blue sky, just like a big mirror. So your friend wasn't totally wrong!

Next time you see a bright blue sky, you can remember that it's because tiny bits of air are bouncing blue light all around, like a giant game of ping-pong with light. Pretty amazing, right?

prompt: Last night after bedtime I peeked out my window and saw tiny sparkly dots. My big brother said they're burning, but they look so far away. Why do stars shine at night?

response.1:
That's a wonderful question! You saw tiny sparkly dots in the sky — those are stars, and they really are very, very far away.

Stars shine because they are giant balls of hot, glowing gas, like a huge fire in space. Inside a star, there is a special process happening all the time, kind of like a very powerful engine that makes it give off light and heat. That light travels all the way across space to reach your eyes at night.

Your big brother is right that stars are burning, but it's not like a fire you see on Earth. It's a much bigger and hotter kind of burning that keeps the star shining for billions of years. Even though they are burning, they are so far away that they just look like tiny, twinkling dots to us.

So, when you look up at the night sky, you are seeing the light from those faraway, giant, glowing balls of gas. It's one of the most amazing things to see! Next time you look, you can try to find the brightest one.

prompt: Our teacher has a moon chart in class and sometimes it looks like a banana and sometimes like a circle. Did someone take bites out of it? Why does the moon change shape?

response.1:
That's a really great question! No, nobody is taking bites out of the moon. The moon doesn't actually change shape at all — it's always a big round ball, like a giant rock in space.

Here's what's happening: The moon goes around the Earth, and the sun shines light on it, just like a big lamp. Sometimes we see the whole sunny side of the moon (that's the full circle), and sometimes we only see part of it (like the banana shape, which is called a crescent).

Think of it like this: if you hold a ball in a dark room and shine a torch on it from the side, you'll only see a bright curve on one side. The rest is in shadow. That's exactly what happens with the moon! As the moon moves around the Earth, we see different amounts of the sunny side.

The banana shape is called a "crescent moon," and the circle is a "full moon." There are other shapes in between too — like a half-moon (which is actually called a "quarter moon").

So your moon chart is showing you the different ways the moon looks from Earth as it travels around us. It's a cool way to keep track of what the moon will look like each night!

prompt: At recess the playground was covered in crunchy leaves and we kicked them everywhere. My friend said the trees are 'going to sleep.' Why do leaves fall in autumn?

response.1:
That sounds like so much fun — kicking crunchy leaves is one of the best parts of autumn! Your friend is right in a way: trees do sort of "go to sleep" in autumn, but let me explain what's really happening.

In spring and summer, trees use sunlight, water, and air to make their own food through their leaves. That's why leaves are green — they have a special green stuff called chlorophyll that helps them make food.

When autumn comes, the days get shorter and colder. The tree knows winter is coming, when there won't be enough sunlight or water to make food. So the tree stops making chlorophyll, and the green color fades away. That's when you see the beautiful yellow, orange, and red colors that were hiding underneath!

Then the tree grows a tiny layer between the leaf and the branch — like a little wall — that slowly cuts off the leaf. When that wall is complete, the leaf has no more connection to the tree, and a gentle breeze or a kick from you sends it floating down.

The tree isn't sad about losing its leaves. It's actually saving energy for winter. In spring, when the weather warms up, the tree will wake up and grow brand-new leaves. So kicking those leaves is like helping the tree get ready for its winter nap!

Next time you're outside, you can look at the bare branches and know the tree is just resting, waiting for spring to come back.

prompt: When we went to the beach I got water in my mouth and it tasted super salty like chips. Nobody put salt in it, so why is the ocean salty?

response.1:
That's a really great question! You're right — the ocean tastes salty, but nobody adds salt to it like you would with food. So where does all that salt come from?

Here's how it works:

1. **Rain and rivers carry tiny bits of salt to the ocean.**  
   Rain is a little bit like weak lemon juice — it's slightly acidic. When rain falls on rocks and soil on land, it slowly breaks tiny pieces off them. Those tiny pieces contain minerals, including salt. Rivers and streams carry those tiny bits of salt into the ocean.

2. **The ocean keeps the salt.**  
   When water from the ocean evaporates (turns into vapor and goes up into the sky to make clouds), the salt stays behind. So over millions and millions of years, the salt has built up in the ocean, making it taste salty.

3. **There are also special places on the ocean floor.**  
   Underwater volcanoes and hot vents release minerals, including salt, directly into the ocean water.

So the ocean is salty because of a very slow, natural process that has been happening for a very long time — like a giant, natural soup that keeps getting saltier and saltier!

Next time you're at the beach, you can tell your friends or family that the salt in the ocean came from rocks on land, carried there by rivers. Pretty cool, right?

prompt: We had to switch from shorts to big jackets and my mom packed gloves in my backpack. Why does the weather change like that? Why do we have seasons?

response.1:
That's a great question! You've noticed something really important about the world around you.

The reason we have seasons – like switching from hot weather to cold weather, or from shorts to big jackets – is because of how our planet Earth moves.

Think of Earth like a spinning top that is also going around the sun. It takes one whole year for Earth to go all the way around the sun. But here's the special part: Earth is tilted a little bit, like it's leaning to one side.

Because of this tilt, different parts of Earth get more or less direct sunlight at different times of the year.

- **When your part of the world is tilted toward the sun**, the sun's rays hit it more directly. That means more warmth and longer days. That's summer! That's when you wear shorts.
- **When your part of the world is tilted away from the sun**, the sun's rays hit it at a slant. That means less warmth and shorter days. That's winter! That's when you need big jackets and gloves.

So, your mom packed your gloves because the part of the world where you live is now tilted away from the sun, making it colder. The seasons change in a big, slow circle every year, just like Earth's trip around the sun.

Isn't it cool that a simple tilt of our planet can make such a big difference? You can even try this at home with a flashlight and a ball to see how the light changes when you tilt it!

prompt: My dad told me not to stare at the sun because it could hurt my eyes. If it's so far away, why is the sun so bright?

response.1:
That's a really smart question! You're right — the sun is very, very far away, about 93 million miles from Earth. But even though it's far, it's also incredibly huge and powerful.

Think of it like this: imagine a giant campfire. If you stand far away from it, you can still feel its warmth and see its light, right? The sun is like a gigantic, super-hot campfire in space. It's so big that more than a million Earths could fit inside it! And it's so hot that it glows brighter than anything else in our sky.

The light from the sun travels all the way to Earth in about 8 minutes. Even though the sun is far, its light is still strong enough to warm our planet and help plants grow. But that same light is also powerful enough to hurt your eyes if you stare right at it — just like you wouldn't stare at a very bright flashlight or a welding torch up close.

So your dad gave you good advice! Looking at the sun can damage your eyes, even if it doesn't hurt right away. If you ever want to look at the sun safely, you need special glasses made for that — never regular sunglasses or binoculars.

If you're curious about the sun, you could ask your dad or teacher to show you a book or a video about it instead. That way you can learn all about it without hurting your eyes!

prompt: After it rained, I saw a rainbow and ran to tell my teacher before it disappeared. Where did it come from? Why do rainbows appear?

response.1:
That's a wonderful question! It's so exciting to see a rainbow after the rain. I'm glad you ran to tell your teacher — that's a great thing to do when you see something amazing.

Here's how rainbows happen, in a simple way:

1. **Sunlight is actually made of many colors.** Even though it looks white or yellow, it's really a mix of all the colors you see in a rainbow: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet.

2. **Raindrops act like tiny prisms.** After it rains, there are still lots of tiny water drops floating in the air. When sunlight passes through these drops, the light bends and splits into all those different colors.

3. **You see the colors as a big arc in the sky.** The raindrops send the colors back to your eyes, and because there are so many drops, you see a giant, colorful curve — a rainbow!

The best time to see a rainbow is when the sun is behind you and the rain is in front of you. That's why they often appear in the morning or late afternoon.

And don't worry — even though a rainbow might seem to disappear quickly, it's not gone forever. Every time the sun comes out after a rain shower, there's a chance you'll see another one. You can even try making your own mini-rainbow with a garden hose on a sunny day!

Next time you see one, you can tell your friends and teacher exactly how it works. Isn't nature amazing?

prompt: At recess I lay on the grass and watched clouds move like cotton balls. They look heavy. Why don’t they fall down? Why do clouds float?

response.1:
That's a really good question! You're right — clouds can look soft and heavy, like big fluffy cotton balls. So why don't they just fall out of the sky?

Here's the simple answer: Clouds are made of tiny, tiny water droplets or ice crystals — so small that you can't even see them one by one. They are much lighter than a single raindrop. And because they are so light, the air around them can hold them up, kind of like how dust floats in a sunbeam.

Think of it like this: when you blow on a feather, it floats up and drifts around. The air is pushing it. The same thing happens with clouds — the air underneath them pushes up gently, and that keeps them floating.

But here's the cool part: when those tiny water droplets bump into each other and grow bigger and heavier, they eventually become too heavy for the air to hold up. That's when they fall as rain! So clouds do fall — just not all at once, and not as big fluffy blobs. They fall as raindrops.

So next time you're lying on the grass watching clouds, you can remember: they're floating because they're made of super-light water bits, and the air is holding them up like an invisible pillow. Pretty amazing, right?

prompt: We had indoor recess because it was pouring outside and I was mad. Who turns the rain on? Why does it rain?

response.1:
That's a great question! I can see why you'd be frustrated about indoor recess — it's no fun when you're stuck inside and really wanted to play outside.

Let me answer your questions:

**Who turns the rain on?**
Nobody turns the rain on like a switch. Rain happens naturally, all by itself. There's no person or button that makes it rain. It's part of how our weather works.

**Why does it rain?**
Here's a simple way to think about it:

1. The sun heats up water from rivers, lakes, and oceans. That water turns into tiny invisible bits called water vapor and rises up into the sky.
2. Up in the sky, the air is cooler. The tiny water bits come together to form clouds.
3. When the clouds get heavy with too much water, the water falls back down as rain.

So rain is really just water taking a trip — from the ground up to the sky, and then back down again!

**What about your mad feeling?**
It's totally okay to feel disappointed when plans change. Next time indoor recess happens, maybe you can think of a fun game to play inside with your friends — like a quiet drawing contest or a card game. And remember, the rain helps plants grow and fills up the water we drink, so it's useful even when it messes up recess!

If you want to learn more about rain or weather, you could ask your teacher or a grown-up at home to show you a book or a kid-friendly video about it.

prompt: I wanted to keep playing my game but my mom said bedtime is important. If I’m not tired yet, why do we even need to sleep?

response.1:
That's a really good question, and a lot of kids wonder the same thing! Even if you don't feel tired, your body and brain still need sleep to work well.

Think of sleep like charging a battery. When you play games, run around, and learn at school, you use up energy. Sleep is when your body recharges. Your brain also uses sleep to sort through everything you learned and saw during the day, like saving important files on a computer.

Even if you don't feel sleepy, your body is still tired. Sometimes kids feel wide awake because they're having fun, but their body is secretly asking for rest. That's why your mom says bedtime is important — she's helping you stay healthy and strong so you can play and learn even better tomorrow.

A good way to wind down is to do something calm before bed, like reading a book or listening to soft music. That helps your brain get ready to sleep, even if you don't feel tired yet.

So, sleep is like a superpower that helps you grow, stay healthy, and have more energy for the things you love — like your game!

prompt: During reading time I yawned and then my friend yawned too. It felt like it spread. Why do we yawn?

response.1:
That's a great observation! Yawning really does feel like it spreads, and you're not alone in noticing that.

Scientists think we yawn for a few reasons. One big reason is to help cool down our brains. When you're tired, bored, or just sitting still for a while, your brain can get a little warm. A big yawn brings in a rush of cool air, which helps your brain feel more awake and ready to focus again.

As for why your friend yawned after you, that's called "contagious yawning." It's something that happens between people who are close or care about each other. Some scientists believe it's a way our brains show empathy — that's the ability to understand and share how someone else is feeling. So when you yawned, your friend's brain kind of "caught" that feeling, and they yawned too. It's like a little sign that you're connected.

So next time it happens, you can smile and know it just means you and your friend are in tune with each other. And if you feel a yawn coming during reading time, it might just be your brain saying, "Time to cool down and get ready to learn!"

prompt: My teacher said blinking keeps our eyes healthy but I don’t even notice doing it. Why do we blink?

response.1:
That's a really great question! Your teacher is right — blinking is super important for your eyes, even though you don't have to think about it.

Here's why we blink:

**1. To keep our eyes wet and clean**
Your eyes need a thin layer of tears on them all the time to stay moist and comfortable. Every time you blink, your eyelids spread fresh tears across your eyes like a tiny windshield wiper. This washes away dust, dirt, and germs that could hurt your eyes.

**2. To protect your eyes**
Blinking is like a quick shield. If something is about to fly into your eye — like a speck of dust or a tiny bug — blinking helps block it. Your eyelids close very fast to keep your eyes safe.

**3. To rest your eyes**
When you blink, your eyes get a tiny break — even if it's just for a split second. This helps stop your eyes from getting too tired, especially when you're reading or looking at a screen.

**Why don't you notice it?**
Your brain is very clever! It makes blinking happen automatically, like breathing or your heart beating. You don't have to remember to do it — your body just does it for you. Most people blink about 15 to 20 times every minute without even thinking about it.

So next time you're in class, you can smile to yourself knowing that your eyes are getting a little wash and rest every few seconds — all thanks to blinking!

prompt: Before lunch my stomach makes growling noises and my friends laugh. Why do we get hungry like that?

response.1:
That’s a great question! That growling noise your stomach makes before lunch is actually a sign that your body is working well. Let me explain what’s happening.

Your stomach is like a busy kitchen. When it’s empty, it still squeezes and moves around to get ready for food. Those squeezes push air and liquid around inside, and that’s what makes the growling sound. It’s called "borborygmi" (say it like bor-bor-RIG-mee), which is just a fancy word for stomach noises.

You get hungry because your body has used up the energy from your last meal. Your brain sends a signal that says, "Hey, it’s time to refuel!" That’s when your stomach starts making those noises to remind you to eat.

Your friends might laugh because the sound is funny or unexpected, but it’s totally normal and healthy. Everyone’s stomach makes noises sometimes — even your friends’ stomachs! You can just smile and say, "My stomach is telling me it’s almost lunchtime!" That way, you turn it into a joke instead of something to feel embarrassed about.

So next time your stomach growls, remember: it’s just your body’s way of saying, "I’m ready for some yummy food!"

prompt: After running laps in gym my legs felt like jelly. Why do we feel tired after running?

response.1:
That's a great question! When you run, your body is working really hard. Let me explain what's happening.

Your muscles are like little engines. To run, they need energy. Your body makes that energy from the food you eat. But when you run fast or for a long time, your muscles use up a lot of that energy really quickly.

Also, when you run, your body makes something called lactic acid. That's a fancy name for a natural thing your muscles create when they work hard. It's what makes your legs feel heavy or like jelly.

Your heart is also pumping extra fast to send oxygen to your legs. And you're breathing harder to get more air. All that hard work is why you feel tired.

The good news is, feeling tired after running is totally normal and actually a good sign! It means you exercised and made your body stronger. After you rest for a little while, drink some water, and maybe have a small snack like a banana or some groundnuts, your legs will start to feel better.

So next time your legs feel like jelly after gym, just remember — your body is getting fitter and stronger!

prompt: In gym class we ran around cones and I could feel my heart thumping in my chest. Why does our heart beat faster when we run?

response.1:
That's a great question! When you run, your body needs more energy to move your legs and arms quickly. Your heart is like a super-strong pump that sends blood all around your body. Blood carries oxygen and food to your muscles so they can work.

When you start running, your muscles shout, "Hey, I need more oxygen and energy right now!" So your brain tells your heart, "Pump faster!" That's why you feel your heart thumping hard in your chest — it's working extra hard to send more blood to your muscles.

Think of it like a car engine revving up when you press the gas pedal. Your heart is revving up to help you run. Once you stop and rest, your heart slows back down because your muscles don't need as much help anymore.

So that thumping feeling is just your amazing heart doing its job to keep you moving and playing. Pretty cool, right?

prompt: I told my mom about a dream where I was flying over school. My brain made it up while I was asleep. Why do we dream?

response.1:
That's a really cool dream — flying over your school sounds amazing! You're right that your brain made it up while you were asleep. Let me explain why we dream.

When you sleep, your brain doesn't just switch off. It stays busy sorting through everything that happened during the day — things you saw, learned, felt, or even worried about. Dreams are like your brain's way of filing and organizing those memories, almost like tidying up a messy room.

Sometimes your brain mixes those memories with feelings or imagination, which is why dreams can be strange or exciting — like flying! Flying dreams are very common and often happen when you're feeling happy, free, or excited about something.

No one knows exactly why we dream, but scientists think dreams help us:
- Practice handling feelings or situations
- Solve little problems in our minds
- Store important memories

So your flying dream might mean your brain was having fun with the idea of being free and happy at school. It's nothing to worry about — just your brain's way of playing while you rest.

If you ever have a dream that scares you or feels too real, you can always tell your mom or dad about it. They can help you feel better. But a flying dream sounds like a good one!

prompt: In class someone sneezed super loud and scared everyone. Why does that happen? Why do we sneeze?

response.1:
That's a great question! It can be surprising when someone sneezes really loudly, especially in a quiet classroom.

**Why do we sneeze?**

A sneeze is your body's way of clearing out your nose. Sometimes tiny things like dust, pollen, or even a tickle from a cold get inside your nose. Your nose doesn't like that, so it sends a fast, strong message to your brain: "Get this out!" Your brain then tells your muscles to take a big breath and then blast the air out through your nose and mouth. That blast is the sneeze! It's like a super-powered nose-cleaning machine.

**Why was it so loud?**

The sound of a sneeze depends on how much air you take in and how fast you push it out. Some people take a really big breath and push it out very hard, which makes a loud "AH-CHOO!" Other people sneeze more quietly. It's just the way their body does it. The loud sound can startle people because it's sudden and unexpected, like a balloon popping.

So, the person who sneezed wasn't trying to scare anyone. Their body just needed to clear their nose in a very powerful way. It's a normal, healthy thing that happens to everyone. Next time someone sneezes loudly, you can just say "Bless you!" and know that their nose just did a great job of cleaning itself.

prompt: At lunch I got hiccups and my friend tried to scare me to fix it. Why do we hiccup anyway?

response.1:
That's a great question! Hiccups can be funny and a little annoying at the same time.

Here’s what’s happening when you hiccup: deep inside your chest, you have a big, flat muscle called the **diaphragm** (say it: DIE-uh-fram). It helps you breathe in and out. Sometimes, that muscle gets a little twitch or spasm, like when your eyelid twitches. When it twitches, it makes you quickly suck in air, and then your vocal cords snap shut, making that "hic!" sound.

Hiccups can start for lots of reasons:
- Eating or drinking too fast
- Eating spicy or very hot food
- Getting excited or laughing hard
- Your tummy being too full or too empty

As for your friend trying to scare you — that's a very old trick people use to try to stop hiccups. Sometimes it works, sometimes it doesn't. But being scared can actually make your body focus on something else, which might help the hiccup twitch stop. Other things that sometimes help are drinking a glass of water slowly, holding your breath for a few seconds, or just waiting — hiccups usually go away on their own after a few minutes.

So next time you get hiccups, you can tell your friend: "It's just my diaphragm having a little twitch!" And if you don't want to be scared, you can just say, "No thanks, I'll just wait for them to stop."

prompt: When it’s cold waiting for the bus, I get tiny bumps on my arms. Why do we get goosebumps?

response.1:
That's a great question! Those tiny bumps on your arms are called **goosebumps** — and they actually happen for a very old reason, from a long time ago when humans had a lot more hair on their bodies.

Here’s what’s going on:

When you’re cold, your brain sends a tiny signal to the tiny muscles at the bottom of each hair on your arm. Those muscles tighten up, which makes the hair stand up straight. That little pull creates the bump you see.

A long, long time ago, when our ancestors had thick fur all over, those raised hairs would trap a layer of warm air next to the skin — like a little blanket. That helped keep them warm. Today, we don’t have enough hair for that to work, but the reflex is still there.

Goosebumps can also happen when you’re scared or really excited — like when you watch a scary movie or hear an amazing song. That’s because the same reflex can be triggered by strong feelings too.

So next time you’re waiting for the bus and see those bumps, you can think: “My body is trying to fluff up my fur to keep me warm — even though I don’t have fur anymore!” It’s just a funny little leftover from our ancient past.

Stay warm out there!

prompt: Our dog’s tail goes crazy when my dad gets home. Is he talking with it? Why do dogs wag their tails?

response.1:
That's a great question! Dogs don't talk with words like we do, but they do use their tails to "talk" in their own way. When your dog's tail wags fast and happily when your dad gets home, it's like the dog is saying, "I'm so happy you're here! I missed you!"

Dogs wag their tails to show how they're feeling. A fast, wiggly wag usually means they're excited or happy. A slow, gentle wag can mean they're feeling calm or friendly. And if the tail is held high and stiff, it might mean the dog is alert or a little unsure.

So your dog isn't using words, but he's definitely telling your dad something special — that he loves him and is glad he's home. Dogs are really good at showing their feelings with their whole body, not just their tail. Their ears, eyes, and even the way they stand can tell you a lot about how they feel.

Next time you see your dog wagging, you can watch his whole body to guess what he's saying. It's like learning a fun secret language!

prompt: When I pet my cat she makes a tiny motor sound. Why do cats purr?

response.1:
That's a great question! That tiny motor sound you hear is called purring, and it's one of the coolest things about cats.

Cats purr for a few different reasons. The most common reason is that they are happy and relaxed. When you pet your cat and she purrs, it's like she's saying, "I love this! Please keep going!" It's her way of showing she feels safe and content with you.

But cats also purr when they are a little bit nervous, hurt, or scared. Scientists think purring might help a cat calm down or even help their body heal a little bit. The vibrations from purring can be soothing, like a gentle massage from the inside.

So, when your cat purrs while you pet her, it's almost always a good sign. She's telling you she trusts you and feels happy in that moment. You're giving her a wonderful feeling, and she's sharing that happy sound with you.

Keep being a kind and gentle friend to your cat, and she'll keep sharing her purrs with you

prompt: We watched birds outside the classroom window and they just flew away. Why can birds fly but we can’t?

response.1:
That's a really good question! Watching birds fly is so cool, isn't it? Let me explain why birds can fly and we can't.

Birds have special bodies that are made for flying. Here are the main reasons:

1. **Wings** – Birds have wings that are shaped like a curve on top and flat on the bottom. When they flap them, air moves faster over the top and slower underneath, which lifts them up. We don't have wings, so we can't push against the air the same way.

2. **Light bones** – Birds have very light, hollow bones. That makes their bodies much lighter than ours. Our bones are heavy and solid, which helps us walk and run, but not fly.

3. **Strong chest muscles** – Birds have very strong muscles in their chests to flap their wings over and over. Our arm muscles aren't built for that kind of work.

4. **Feathers** – Feathers are light and help birds catch the air. They also keep birds warm and dry. We don't have feathers.

So even though we can't fly like birds, we have our own special abilities! We can run, jump, swim, climb, and use our hands to build things. People have even invented airplanes and helicopters so we can travel through the sky too — just in a different way.

Next time you see birds flying, you can remember all the amazing things their bodies can do that ours can't. And you can also think about all the amazing things your body can do that theirs can't!

prompt: On our aquarium trip the fish never came out of the water. Why do fish live in water all the time?

response.1:
That's a really good question! You noticed something important on your aquarium trip.

Fish live in water all the time because their bodies are made especially for living underwater. They have gills instead of lungs like we do. Gills are like special filters that take oxygen out of the water so the fish can breathe. If a fish came out of the water, its gills would dry out and it wouldn't be able to get any oxygen, just like we can't breathe underwater.

Fish also have fins and a tail to help them swim, and their bodies are covered in scales and slime that protect them and help them glide through the water. They are perfectly built to be underwater, just like birds are perfectly built to fly in the air.

So the fish at the aquarium weren't hiding from you — they were just doing what fish do best, living happily in their watery home. Next time you visit, you can watch how they use their fins and gills to move and breathe. It's pretty amazing!

prompt: Our science book said bees make honey for themselves. Why do bees make honey?

response.1:
That's a great question! Your science book is right — bees make honey for themselves, but it also helps us in a wonderful way.

Bees make honey as their own food supply. They store it inside their hive to eat during times when there aren't many flowers, like in the rainy season or when it's very dry. Honey gives them energy to fly, build their hive, and take care of their babies.

Here's how they do it:

- Worker bees fly from flower to flower, sipping a sweet liquid called nectar with their long tongues.
- They carry the nectar back to the hive in a special "honey stomach."
- Inside the hive, other bees pass the nectar from mouth to mouth, which changes it into honey.
- They fan it with their wings to make it thicker and then seal it in little wax cells with a wax cap.

So honey is really the bees' own food — like a pantry full of snacks for the whole colony!

The extra honey that bees make is what people collect. Beekeepers take only a little bit, making sure to leave enough for the bees to eat. That's why we can enjoy honey on bread or in tea without hurting the bees.

Isn't it amazing how such tiny creatures work together to make something so sweet?

prompt: My teacher said bears sleep all winter. Why do some animals hibernate?

response.1:
That's a great question! Your teacher is right — bears do sleep for a long time during winter, and that's called hibernation. Let me explain why some animals do this.

Hibernation is like a very deep, long nap that helps animals survive when it gets very cold and food becomes hard to find. In winter, there are no berries, leaves, or insects to eat, and the ground might be covered in snow. So animals like bears, hedgehogs, and some bats go into a special sleep to save energy.

During hibernation, their body slows down a lot. Their heart beats much slower, they breathe less often, and their body temperature drops. This way, they don't need to eat for months because they use the fat they stored up during summer and autumn.

Think of it like this: before winter comes, animals eat extra food to build up fat — like packing a lunchbox for the whole winter! Then they find a safe, warm place like a cave, a burrow, or a hollow tree, curl up, and sleep until spring arrives with fresh food again.

Not all animals hibernate the same way. Bears sleep deeply but can wake up if they need to. Some small animals like groundhogs go into an even deeper sleep that's harder to wake from.

So hibernation is really a clever way animals have learned to survive when the weather gets tough and food is scarce. Isn't nature amazing?

prompt: I saw a giraffe video and its neck was super long. Why do giraffes have long necks?

response.1:
That's a great question! Giraffes have such long necks for a few important reasons.

First, their long necks help them reach leaves high up in trees that other animals can't get to. This means they have plenty of food all to themselves. They especially love eating leaves from acacia trees.

Second, a male giraffe uses its neck to fight other males. They swing their heads and necks at each other to show who is strongest. This is called "necking."

Third, having a long neck helps them see far across the grasslands. They can spot lions or other danger from far away, which helps them stay safe.

So a giraffe's long neck is like a special tool that helps it eat, fight, and stay safe all at once. Pretty cool, right?

prompt: Penguins have wings but they just waddle. Why don’t penguins fly?

response.1:
That's a really great question! Penguins do have wings, but they use them in a very special way.

Penguins are birds that are built for swimming instead of flying. Their wings are shaped more like flippers, and they are very strong. When penguins are in the water, they flap their flippers to "fly" through the ocean really fast. They can zoom around to catch fish and escape from seals.

So, why don't they fly in the air? A long, long time ago, penguins' ancestors could fly. But over millions of years, they started spending more and more time in the cold water looking for food. Their bodies changed to be better swimmers. Their wings got smaller and stronger for paddling, and their bodies got heavier and more streamlined for diving. Flying takes a lot of energy, and for penguins, it became better to be amazing swimmers than okay fliers.

Think of it like this: a penguin's wings are like a swimmer's flippers, not like an eagle's wings. They are perfect for what penguins need to do every day—hunt for food in the ocean. So, they don't fly in the sky, but they are the best "flyers" underwater!

prompt: We saw a frog near the sidewalk and it bounced away fast. Why do frogs jump instead of walk?

response.1:
That's a great question! Frogs jump instead of walking because their bodies are built for it.

Frogs have very strong back legs and big feet. Their legs work like springs. When a frog wants to move, it bends its legs and then pushes off the ground really hard. That's why they can jump so far and so fast!

Jumping helps frogs in two big ways:

1. **To escape danger** – If a frog sees something that might eat it (like a bird or a snake), jumping away quickly helps it get to safety. A fast jump is much harder to catch than a slow walk.

2. **To catch food** – Frogs eat bugs like flies and mosquitoes. Jumping lets them surprise their food and grab it with their long, sticky tongue.

Some frogs can jump more than 20 times their own body length! That would be like you jumping across a whole swimming pool in one go.

So the frog you saw was probably just doing what frogs do best – using its super-strong legs to bounce away and stay safe. Next time you see one, you can watch how it uses those springy legs to move around.

prompt: In the school garden I saw butterflies with bright colors. Why do butterflies have colorful wings?

response.1:
That's a great question! Butterflies have bright, colorful wings for a few important reasons.

First, the colors help them stay safe. Some butterflies have bright colors that warn birds and other animals, "Hey, I don't taste good!" So the animals learn to leave them alone.

Second, the colors help butterflies find each other. When a butterfly sees another butterfly with the same bright pattern, it knows, "That's one of my kind!" This helps them find a friend to have baby butterflies with.

Third, some butterflies have colors that look like big eyes or scary patterns. This can trick a hungry bird into thinking the butterfly is a bigger, scarier animal, so the bird flies away.

The colors come from tiny scales on their wings, like little tiles on a roof. Some colors are made by special chemicals in the scales, and some are made by the way light bounces off the scales — kind of like how a soap bubble can look rainbow-colored.

Next time you see a butterfly in your school garden, you can watch it and think about all the clever ways its wings help it survive and find friends. Isn't nature amazing?

prompt: My teacher gave us math homework again and I groaned. Why do we have homework?

response.1:
That's a really good question, and you're not alone in feeling that way. Lots of kids groan when they hear the word "homework"!

Homework is like practice for your brain, just like how you practice a sport or a musical instrument to get better. When your teacher gives you math homework, it's a chance to try the problems on your own, in a quiet place, without anyone rushing you. It helps you remember what you learned in class and makes those math muscles stronger.

Think of it this way: in class, your teacher shows you how to do something new. Homework is your chance to say, "Okay, I think I've got it!" and try it yourself. If you get stuck, that's actually helpful too, because then you know what to ask your teacher about the next day.

So, while it might not be the most fun part of your day, homework is a tool to help you learn and feel more confident. A good way to handle it is to take a short break after school, have a snack, and then do your homework when you feel ready. If you ever find it too hard or too much, you can always tell your parents or your teacher. They want to help you succeed!

prompt: We do so many math problems every day. Why do we learn math?

response.1:
That's a really great question! Math can feel like a lot of work sometimes, but it's actually one of the most useful things you learn in school. Here's why:

**Math helps you solve real-life problems every day.**

- When you share snacks with friends, you're using division.
- When you save your pocket money to buy something, you're using addition and subtraction.
- When you check the time to know when your favourite show starts, you're using math.
- When you help measure ingredients for cooking or baking at home, that's math too.

**Math teaches your brain to think clearly.**

- It helps you notice patterns, like how the days of the week repeat or how numbers grow.
- It helps you figure out tricky problems step by step, which is useful for all kinds of things — even games and puzzles.

**Math is used in many cool jobs.**

- Doctors use math to give the right medicine.
- Engineers use math to build bridges and cars.
- Artists and musicians use math to make things look and sound beautiful.
- Even farmers use math to know how much seed or water their crops need.

So even though it can feel like a lot of practice, every problem you solve is helping your brain get stronger and preparing you for all sorts of things you'll do in life. Keep going — you're doing great!

prompt: My mom makes me read before bed even when I want to watch cartoons. Why do we need to read books?

response.1:
That's a really good question, and I can see why you'd rather watch cartoons — cartoons are fun and exciting! But reading books before bed is actually something special that helps you in a few cool ways.

First, reading helps your brain get ready for sleep. When you watch cartoons, the bright lights and fast-moving pictures can keep your brain awake and make it harder to fall asleep. But when you read a book, your brain calms down, and it's easier to drift off to dreamland.

Second, reading is like exercise for your imagination. When you read, you get to picture the characters, the places, and the adventures all in your own head. It's like you're the director of your own movie! Cartoons show you everything, but books let you create the world yourself.

Third, the more you read, the better you get at it — and that helps you in school, with your homework, and even with understanding new things. It's like building a superpower for your brain.

Maybe you could ask your mom if you can watch one short cartoon first, and then read for a little while before bed. That way you get both! Or you could pick a book that feels like an adventure, so reading feels more like fun and less like a chore.

Reading is a gift your mom is giving you, even if it doesn't feel like it right now. One day, you might even thank her for it!

prompt: Everyone gets nervous before a test in class. Why do teachers give tests?

response.1:
That's a really good question, and you're right — almost everyone feels a little nervous before a test. That's totally normal!

Teachers give tests for a few important reasons:

1. **To see what you've learned** – Tests help teachers know which parts of a lesson you understand well and which parts might need a little more practice. It's like a check-up for your brain!

2. **To help you remember** – When you study for a test and then answer questions, it helps your brain store that information for a long time. It's like practicing a football drill or a dance move until you can do it without thinking.

3. **To help you get better at showing what you know** – Tests also teach you how to read questions carefully, manage your time, and stay calm under pressure. These are skills that will help you in many things, not just school.

4. **To help your teacher plan** – After a test, your teacher can see which topics the whole class needs to go over again, and which students might need extra help or more challenging work.

Think of a test like a friendly game or a quiz show — it's not meant to trick you, but to show how much you've grown. And if you feel nervous, that's okay! Taking a few deep breaths, getting a good night's sleep, and telling yourself "I've done my best to prepare" can really help.

If you ever feel too worried about a test, you can always talk to your teacher, your parents, or an older sibling or auntie or uncle. They can help you find ways to feel more ready and calm.

prompt: Sometimes I want to stay home and play games instead of going to school. Why do we have to go every day?

response.1:
That's a really good question, and I think a lot of kids feel the same way sometimes! Playing games is fun, and staying home sounds cozy. But school is important for a few big reasons, even if it doesn't always feel that way.

Think of school like a place where you get to build your brain and learn superpowers for life. Every day, you learn new things – like how to read better, solve tricky math problems, or understand how the world works. These are skills you'll use for the rest of your life, just like leveling up in a game.

School also helps you learn how to be with other people. You get to make friends, work in groups, share ideas, and learn to be patient and kind. These are really important skills for when you grow up, whether you want to be a doctor, a teacher, a pilot, or anything else.

And here's a secret: going to school every day helps you build a good habit. It's like practicing something until it becomes easy. The more you go, the more you learn, and the stronger your brain gets.

It's totally okay to wish for a day off sometimes. Maybe you can talk to your parents or the grown-up who takes care of you about having a special "rest and play" day during a school holiday. But for now, think of school as your main adventure – a place where you're getting stronger and smarter every single day. You've got this!

prompt: My friend at recess said water isn’t really wet and we argued about it. So why is water wet?

response.1:
That's a really fun question, and it's one that even scientists sometimes argue about! Let's break it down in a simple way.

**What does "wet" mean?**

When we say something is "wet," we usually mean that a liquid, like water, is sticking to its surface. For example, if you spill water on your shirt, the water sticks to the fabric, and you say your shirt is wet.

**So, is water itself wet?**

Here's the tricky part: Water is a liquid. For water to be "wet," it would need to have water sticking to it. But water can't stick to itself in the same way it sticks to your shirt.

Think of it like this:
- If you put your hand in a bucket of water, your hand gets wet because the water sticks to your skin.
- But if you look at a single drop of water, it's just water. It doesn't have another liquid sticking to it.

**The simple answer most scientists agree on:**

Water itself is **not** wet. Water is the thing that makes other things wet. It's the "wetter," not the "wet."

**But your friend has a point too!**

Some people say water *is* wet because when you have a lot of water together, the water molecules (the tiny, tiny pieces that make up water) are touching each other. So in a way, the water is "wetting" itself.

**The best way to settle the argument:**

You can both be right, depending on how you look at it! The most common way to think about it is:

- **Water makes things wet.**
- **Water itself is not wet.**

So next time you and your friend talk about it, you can say, "Water is the reason my shirt is wet, but the water itself is just water!" It's a great way to think about science and words at the same time.

prompt: I put an ice cube in my drink and it disappeared. Why does ice melt?

response.1:
That's a great observation! You're right — the ice cube didn't really disappear, it just changed form.

Ice is frozen water. When you put it in your drink, the drink is warmer than the ice. The cold from the ice moves into the drink, and the warmth from the drink moves into the ice. This warmth makes the ice turn back into liquid water. That's called melting.

Think of it like this: ice is water that's been cooled so much it becomes solid. When it gets warm again, it goes back to being liquid. The water from the melted ice is still in your drink — you just can't see it as a cube anymore.

So next time you see an ice cube "disappear," you'll know it's just turning back into water and mixing with your drink. Pretty cool, right?

prompt: At a campfire my dad said not to touch the flames. Why is fire so hot?

response.1:
That's a great question! Fire is hot because of something called a chemical reaction. When things like wood or paper burn, tiny pieces inside them called atoms mix with oxygen from the air really fast. This mixing releases a lot of energy, and that energy comes out as heat and light.

Think of it like this: when you rub your hands together really fast, they get warm, right? Fire is like that, but millions of times faster and stronger. The heat is what makes the fire glow and feel so hot.

Your dad was very smart to tell you not to touch the flames. Fire is so hot that it can hurt your skin very quickly. It's like touching a very hot stove or boiling water. That's why we always stay a safe distance away from campfires and let grown-ups handle them.

If you want to feel the warmth of a campfire, it's best to sit a little bit back and hold your hands out toward it, but never touch the flames or the hot logs. Always ask a grown-up if you're not sure about something near the fire.

prompt: In science class the magnet stuck to my locker but not my notebook. Why do magnets stick to some things?

response.1:
That's a great observation! Magnets stick to things that are made of certain metals, like iron, nickel, or cobalt. Your locker is probably made of steel, and steel has iron in it, so the magnet sticks to it. Your notebook is made of paper, which doesn't have any of those metals, so the magnet just slides right off.

Think of it like this: magnets have a special invisible force field around them. When that force field meets something with iron inside, it pulls them together. But if there's no iron, the force field can't grab on, so nothing happens.

You can test this at home or school! Try your magnet on a paperclip, a coin, a spoon, a plastic cup, or a wooden pencil. You'll see that it only sticks to the metal things that have iron in them. Some coins, like the old Nigerian kobo coins, might stick, but newer ones might not. It's a fun experiment to try!

prompt: When I walk under the streetlight at night, a dark shape follows me. Why do shadows appear?

response.1:
That's a great question! Shadows can look a little spooky at night, but they're actually just a normal part of how light works.

A shadow appears when something blocks light. During the day, the sun is a big light source, so everything around you makes shadows. At night, streetlights are smaller light sources, so the shadows are sharper and can look like they're following you.

Here's the simple reason: when you walk under a streetlight, your body blocks the light from reaching the ground behind you. That dark shape you see is your own shadow! It follows you because you are the one blocking the light. If you stop, it stops. If you move, it moves with you.

Think of it like this: if you hold a toy in front of a flashlight on the wall, the toy's shadow moves whenever you move the toy. You are the toy, and the streetlight is the flashlight.

So next time you see that dark shape, remember: it's just your own shadow saying hello. It can't hurt you, and it's always with you when there's a light behind you. If you ever feel nervous, you can walk a little faster or stay near a grown-up, but there's nothing to worry about.

prompt: At my birthday party the balloons went up to the ceiling and stayed there. Why do balloons float?

response.1:
That's a great question! Balloons float because they are filled with a special gas that is lighter than the air around us.

Think of it like this: the air around you is made of tiny, invisible things called molecules. Some gases are made of molecules that are very light and spread out. When a balloon is filled with a gas like helium, the gas inside is much lighter than the air outside. Because it's lighter, it gets pushed up by the heavier air, just like a piece of wood floats to the top of water.

So, the heavier air pushes the lighter balloon up toward the ceiling. That's why your birthday balloons floated up and stayed there! If you let the gas out, the balloon would fall back down because it's no longer lighter than the air.

Next time you see a balloon floating, you'll know it's because the gas inside is lighter than the air around it. Pretty cool, right?

prompt: My friends started giggling in class and then I couldn’t stop laughing either. Why do we laugh?

response.1:
That's a great question! Laughing is something everyone does, and it can be really fun — especially when you're with friends.

Here’s why we laugh:

1. **It’s a way to connect.** When you and your friends laugh together, it makes you feel closer and happier. It’s like your brains are saying, “We’re having fun together!”

2. **It helps you feel good.** Laughing releases special chemicals in your brain that make you feel happy and relaxed. That’s why it’s hard to stop once you start!

3. **It can be contagious.** When you hear someone else laugh, your brain wants to join in — even if you don’t know exactly what’s funny. That’s probably what happened in your class. Your friends started giggling, and your brain said, “That sounds fun, I’ll join in!”

4. **It’s a way to share a moment.** Sometimes laughing together is just a way of saying, “We’re all in this together,” even if the joke is small or silly.

So next time you and your friends get the giggles in class, it’s totally normal. Just try to keep it quiet so your teacher doesn’t get too confused! 😊

prompt: I dropped my pencil in class and it fell to the floor. Why do things fall down instead of up?

response.1:
That's a great question! Things fall down because of something called **gravity**.

Gravity is a force that pulls everything toward the center of the Earth. It's like a giant, invisible magnet that pulls everything—pencils, balls, even you—toward the ground. That's why when you drop your pencil, it always falls down and never up.

If there were no gravity, everything would just float around, like astronauts in space! But here on Earth, gravity keeps us and everything else firmly on the ground.

So next time you drop your pencil, you can remember: gravity is the invisible force that brought it down!

prompt: My dad said the car won’t move unless we put gas in it. Why do cars need fuel?

response.1:
That's a great question! Your dad is right — cars need fuel, like petrol or diesel, to move. Let me explain why.

Think of a car like a toy that needs batteries to work. Without batteries, the toy can't move or make sounds. A car is the same way — it needs fuel to give it energy.

Inside the car is an engine, which is like the car's "muscle." The fuel goes into the engine and burns in a very small, controlled way. That burning creates a tiny explosion that pushes parts inside the engine. Those parts spin the wheels, and that's what makes the car go forward or backward.

So, fuel is the car's food! Just like you need to eat breakfast to have energy to run and play, a car needs fuel to have energy to drive. When the fuel runs out, the car has no more energy, so it stops — just like you might feel tired and need to rest or eat again.

That's why your dad has to stop at a filling station to put more petrol or diesel in the car. It's like giving the car its lunch so it can keep going!

prompt: The dentist said I have to brush or I’ll get cavities. Why do we brush our teeth?

response.1:
That's a great question! The dentist is right — brushing your teeth is super important, and here’s why.

Your mouth is like a busy little house where food and germs live. After you eat, tiny bits of food stay on your teeth. Germs called bacteria love to eat that leftover food. When they eat, they make a sticky, clear film called plaque. Plaque is like a blanket of germs on your teeth.

If you don’t brush, the germs in plaque make a kind of acid that can eat a tiny hole in your tooth. That hole is called a cavity. Cavities can hurt and make your tooth sore. The dentist has to fix them with a filling.

Brushing your teeth twice a day with fluoride toothpaste does three important things:
- It scrubs away the food and plaque.
- It makes your mouth feel fresh and clean.
- The fluoride in the toothpaste helps make your teeth stronger, so they can fight off the germs.

Think of brushing like giving your teeth a bath. You wash your body to stay clean and healthy, and brushing keeps your teeth clean and healthy too.

So keep up the good work! Brush for two minutes every morning and every night, and don’t forget to brush the backs of your teeth and your tongue. Your teeth will thank you with a big, strong smile. 😊

prompt: We have a plant by the classroom window and the teacher said it needs sun to grow. Why do plants need sunlight?

response.1:
That's a great question! Plants need sunlight because they use it to make their own food. It's a bit like how you need to eat breakfast to have energy for the day — except plants make their own breakfast using sunlight, water, and air.

Inside the leaves, there's a special green thing called **chlorophyll** (say: KLOR-uh-fill). It's what makes leaves green. When sunlight hits the leaf, the chlorophyll catches the light and helps the plant turn water and a gas from the air (called carbon dioxide) into sugar. That sugar is the plant's food, and it gives the plant energy to grow, make flowers, and stay healthy.

This process is called **photosynthesis** (say: fo-to-SIN-thuh-sis). It's a big word, but it just means "making food with light."

So when your teacher puts the plant by the sunny window, it's like giving the plant its lunchbox! Without sunlight, the plant can't make food, and it would get weak and stop growing.

You can even try a little experiment: put one plant in a sunny spot and another in a dark cupboard for a few days. The sunny one will stay green and strong, while the dark one will turn pale and droopy. Just make sure to bring the dark one back to the sun so it can recover!

If you want to help your class plant, you can gently turn it every few days so all sides get sunlight. And don't forget to water it a little, too — plants need both sun and water to make their food.

prompt: My clock makes a tick-tock sound at night and I can hear it when I’m trying to sleep. Why do clocks tick?

response.1:
That's a great question! Many clocks with hands (the kind that have a round face with numbers) make a tick-tock sound. Here's why:

Inside the clock, there's a special part called a **pendulum** or a **gear** that moves back and forth. Each time it moves, it makes a little click. That click is the "tick" or the "tock" you hear. The clock uses those ticks to measure exactly one second each time.

So the tick-tock is just the clock's way of counting seconds as it works to tell you the right time.

If the sound bothers you at night, here are a few things you can try:

- Move the clock to another room or farther from your bed.
- Put a soft cloth or towel under the clock to muffle the sound.
- Ask a parent or older sibling if you can use a quiet digital clock instead (those don't tick).
- Try playing soft music or a white noise app on a phone or tablet to cover the sound.

The tick-tock is nothing to worry about — it just means your clock is working properly!

prompt: My mom says I can’t just run outside in my pajamas. Why do we wear clothes?

response.1:
That's a great question! Your mom is right that we don't usually run outside in our pajamas, and there are a few simple reasons why we wear clothes.

First, clothes protect us. They keep us warm when it's cold and shield our skin from the sun when it's hot. They also help keep us safe from scratches, bugs, and dirt when we're playing outside.

Second, clothes help us show respect for ourselves and others. In Nigeria, it's a sign of good training (what some people call *ọmọlúwàbí*) to be properly dressed when you go out. It shows you care about yourself and the people around you. That's why we wear nice clothes to school, to church or mosque, and when visiting family or friends.

Third, clothes are a way to express who we are. You might wear your favorite jersey, a colorful Ankara print, or a simple T-shirt and shorts. What you wear can show your personality, your mood, or even celebrate a special occasion like Sallah or Christmas.

So, wearing clothes isn't just about covering up—it's about staying safe, being respectful, and having fun with your style. And that's why your mom wants you to change out of your pajamas before heading outside!

prompt: At my friend’s birthday party we sang and ate cake and gave presents. Why do we celebrate birthdays every year?

response.1:
That sounds like a lovely birthday party! Singing, eating cake, and giving presents are some of the best parts.

People celebrate birthdays every year for a few simple reasons:

1. **To say "thank you" for being alive.** A birthday is a special day to celebrate that you were born and that you are here with your family and friends. It's like a yearly "happy you day!"

2. **To show love and appreciation.** When we give presents, sing, and share cake, we are telling the birthday person, "You are important to us, and we are glad you are in our lives."

3. **To have fun and make happy memories.** Birthdays are a time to gather with the people we care about, play games, eat special food, and laugh together. These happy memories last a long time.

4. **To mark growing up.** Each birthday is a way of saying, "You are one year older and one year wiser!" It's a chance to look back at all the fun things you did in the past year and look forward to the new year ahead.

So, every year, a birthday is a special tradition that helps us celebrate life, love, and the people we care about. It's a wonderful way to make someone feel special and loved.

prompt: In my class some kids speak another language at home and their parents sound different on the phone. Why do people have different languages?

response.1:
That's a really great question! People have different languages because of how human communities grew and spread out across the world over thousands of years.

Think of it like this: a long, long time ago, groups of people lived together in one place. They made up sounds and words to talk to each other about food, weather, family, and feelings. Over time, some groups moved far away to new lands—across mountains, rivers, or oceans. They didn't see the other groups anymore, so they started making up new words and ways of speaking. After many, many years, their language became completely different from the one the first group spoke.

That's why today we have languages like English, Yoruba, Hausa, Igbo, French, Arabic, and hundreds more. Each one is like a special treasure from a group of people's history and culture.

It's really cool that some kids in your class speak another language at home! That means they can understand and talk to people in two different ways—that's a superpower. And when you hear their parents speaking differently on the phone, it's just their own special language that they grew up with.
